questions.prompt: A UTI can be caused by E. coli, S. aureus, or Pseudomonas. Which limitation of Koch's postulates does this illustrate?

options.text: Some microbes can't be grown in pure culture
Some pathogens only infect humans
Some diseases have more than one possible cause
Some experiments would be unethical

questions.explanation: Koch's postulates assume one microbe → one disease; sinusitis and UTIs have several possible causes.

questions.prompt: A woman takes a long course of antibiotics for strep throat and then develops a vaginal yeast infection. What is the best explanation?

options.text: Candida made bacteriocins that destroyed the antibiotic in the vagina
Strep bacteria moved to the vagina and turned into yeast cells there
The antibiotics killed Lactobacillus, so vaginal pH rose and Candida grew
The antibiotics fed Candida directly, so it multiplied in the vagina

questions.explanation: Lactobacillus normally keeps the vagina at pH ~4–5; without it, pH returns toward 7.35, which Candida likes.

questions.prompt: Which pairing of microbe, location, and relationship is correct?

options.text: E. coli in the colon — parasitic; in the bladder — mutualistic partner
Vibrio cholerae in the intestine — mutualistic; on the skin — parasitic
Candida on the skin — parasitic; in the vagina — mutualistic partner
S. aureus on unbroken skin — commensal; in a surgical wound — opportunist

questions.explanation: Where a microbe lives can change its relationship with the host.

questions.prompt: Why are females more likely than males to get E. coli UTIs?

options.text: Males carry S. epidermidis in the bladder, which blocks E. coli
E. coli only grows at the slightly higher female body temperature
Females have no Lactobacillus anywhere in the urinary tract
The anus is close to the urethral opening and the urethra is short

questions.explanation: Short distances let E. coli reach the bladder — hence wiping front to back.

questions.prompt: A clinic reports a sudden rise in new flu cases this month, but the number of people living with chronic hepatitis is unchanged. Which measures are changing?

options.text: Flu incidence is rising; hepatitis prevalence is steady
Both incidences are falling
Both prevalences are steady
Flu prevalence is falling; hepatitis incidence is rising

questions.explanation: Incidence tracks new cases (spread); prevalence counts all current cases (burden).

questions.prompt: Which statement about the stages of infectious disease is FALSE?

options.text: Signs and symptoms are most severe during the prodromal period.
During convalescence the patient feels normal but microbes may remain.
Death, if it occurs, tends to happen near the peak of the period of illness.
There are no signs or symptoms during incubation.
During decline, the immune system or drugs reduce microbe numbers.

questions.explanation: The prodromal period brings mild signs and symptoms; the period of illness is the most severe.

questions.prompt: Tuberculosis slowly scars the alveoli over years. Which two terms describe it best?

options.text: Chronic and communicable
Sporadic and acute
Acute and non-communicable
Latent and subclinical

questions.explanation: TB develops slowly and lasts long (chronic) and spreads between people.

questions.prompt: Which situation best shows herd immunity?

options.text: A patient recovers from measles and is then immune to it for the rest of her life
A hospital isolates a measles patient in a negative-pressure room for two weeks
An unvaccinated infant avoids measles because most people around her are immune
A vaccinated adult catches a mild case of the flu but recovers within a few days

questions.explanation: When most of a population is immune, the pathogen can't spread to the few who aren't.

questions.prompt: Measles causes spots all over the body. Which term pair fits?

options.text: Local and latent
Systemic and contagious
Local and non-communicable
Systemic and non-communicable

questions.explanation: Systemic = throughout the body; measles spreads easily.

questions.prompt: A nurse notes a blood pressure of 85/50 and a temperature of 104 °F in a patient with bacteria in the blood. What is the best description?

options.text: A local infection confined to one site
Bacteremia leading to sepsis (septic shock)
A subclinical infection without symptoms
Toxemia with no immune response at all

questions.explanation: Sepsis is an extreme immune reaction to pathogens/toxins; septic shock includes a drop in blood pressure.

questions.prompt: Which of these would the course list as a predisposing factor for pneumonia?

options.text: Old age
Having S. epidermidis on the skin
Being the last child in a family
Female sex

questions.explanation: Age is a predisposing factor; female sex is the lecture's predisposing factor for UTIs.

questions.prompt: Why does the lecture say the last child in a family often has the most diverse microbiome?

options.text: Last children receive more antibiotics, which diversify their flora
Parents are less overprotective, so the child meets more microbes early
Older siblings remove the baby's normal flora, so new species move in
Later children are usually born by C-section, which adds more microbes

questions.explanation: More early exposure → more species → more microbial antagonism.

questions.prompt: Which is a SYMPTOM a nurse must ask the patient about?

options.text: A rash
Elevated blood pressure
A measured fever
Malaise

questions.explanation: Symptoms are felt by the patient; signs are observed or measured.

questions.prompt: Explain the difference between a passive carrier and an asymptomatic (active) carrier, with an example of each.
questions.explanation: Textbook Ch. 16: a passive carrier is contaminated but not infected and spreads the pathogen mechanically (a health-care worker who doesn't wash hands). An asymptomatic carrier is infected and transmits the pathogen without showing signs or symptoms — e.g., Typhoid Mary (Salmonella typhi).

questions.prompt: Describe how a newborn acquires L. acidophilus, S. epidermidis, and E. coli, and one consequence of not yet having E. coli.
questions.explanation: L. acidophilus from vaginal delivery; S. epidermidis from nursing and skin-to-skin handling; E. coli from contaminated food and objects. Without E. coli the newborn can't make enough vitamin K, so it gets a vitamin K injection.
